messages.content:
Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Here’s a high‑level workflow you could automate with the two tools you described: | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **1. Discover the ordering API** | Use the *search* tool to query “McDonald’s online ordering API” or “McDonald’s menu API”. | McDonald’s doesn’t publish a public API, so you’ll likely find either an internal endpoint (e.g., `https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu`) or a third‑party service such as DoorDash/UberEats that exposes McDonald’s menu. | | **2. Inspect the API contract** | Once you have the endpoint URL, use the *search* tool again to fetch the OpenAPI/Swagger spec or read the documentation page. | You need to know the exact request format, required headers, authentication method, and the IDs for menu items. | | **3. Resolve authentication** | Identify how the API expects you to authenticate (OAuth2 token, API key, or session cookie). | Without a valid token you can’t place an order. | | **4. Build the order payload** | Create a JSON object that contains:
• `location_id` (or latitude/longitude)
• `items`: array of `{item_id, quantity}`
• `payment_method` (card token or stored payment profile)
• `delivery_address` or `pickup_location`. | This is the core of the order. | | **5. Execute the API call** | Call the *execute* tool with the string representation of the HTTP request:
`POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders`
Headers: `Authorization: Bearer `, `Content-Type: application/json`
Body: the JSON payload from step 4. | This actually places the order. | | **6. Handle the response** | Parse the JSON response. It will contain an `order_id`, status, estimated pickup/delivery time, and any error messages. | You can confirm success or retry on failure. | | **7. Confirm the order** | Optionally, make a `GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders/` to poll status until it’s `completed` or `delivered`. | Gives you real‑time updates. | ### Example (pseudo‑code) ```python # 1. Search for the API search_result = search("McDonald’s online ordering API") api_url = search_result["menu_endpoint"] # e.g., https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu # 2. Get menu items menu_response = execute(f"GET {api_url}") burger_id = next(item["id"] for item in menu_response["items"] if item["name"] == "Burger") fries_id = next(item["id"] for item in menu_response["items"] if item["name"] == "Fries") # 3. Build order payload order_payload = { "location_id": "12345", "items": [ {"item_id": burger_id, "quantity": 1}, {"item_id": fries_id, "quantity": 1} ], "payment_method": {"type": "card", "token": ""}, "delivery_address": {"street": "123 Main St", "city": "Anytown", "zip": "12345"} } # 4. Execute order order_response = execute( f"POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders\n" f"Authorization: Bearer \n" f"Content-Type: application/json\n\n" f"{json.dumps(order_payload)}" ) print(order_response["order_id"], order_response["status"]) ``` ### Things to watch out for | Issue | Mitigation | |-------|------------| | **No public API** | Use a third‑party aggregator (DoorDash, UberEats) that has a documented API. | | **Authentication** | Store OAuth tokens securely; refresh them when they expire. | | **Item IDs** | Cache the menu locally to avoid repeated lookups. | | **Rate limits** | Respect `Retry-After` headers; back‑off on 429 responses. | | **Payment security** | Never store raw card numbers; use tokenization services. | | **Error handling** | Map API error codes to user‑friendly messages. | With this approach you can fully automate the “burger + fries” order: discover the API, build the request, execute it, and confirm the result—all using the two tools you mentioned.
